Female Ornate jobfish (Pristipomoides argyrogrammicus) reach a maximum total body length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters], a size that reflects the species' position as a moderately large-bodied lutjanid inhabiting the deep slopes of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs. This ultimate length is attained after a prolonged growth period that spans much of the animal's life, with the oldest individuals recorded exceeding four decades. At a stable ambient temperature of 20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C], field surveys and laboratory holding studies have documented a maximum lifespan of 14,600 days [am = 14,600 days], a remarkably long duration for a teleost of this body plan and indicative of a slow-paced life history strategy. Such extended longevity is thought to be linked to the stable, low-energy environment of the mesophotic zone, where natural mortality from predation is reduced and metabolic demands are comparatively modest. The combination of large body size and advanced age places this species among the longer-lived members of the genus Pristipomoides, with life-history characteristics that render it particularly vulnerable to overfishing and slow to recover from population depletion.

Growth to the initial size at which female Ornate jobfish attain sexual maturity occurs considerably earlier than the achievement of maximum size. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development and the capacity to participate in spawning aggregations, is reached at a total length of 20 centimeters [Lp = 20 centimeters]. This body length corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 121 grams [Wwp = 121 grams], a threshold that marks the transition from the immature juvenile phase to the reproductively active adult stage. The weight-length relationship underlying this value, derived from extensive morphometric sampling across the species' range, indicates a robust, deep-bodied conformation typical of benthic predatory lutjanids. Females at this size are capable of contributing to the annual spawning biomass, though first-time spawners often produce smaller clutches than larger, more experienced individuals. The documented size at maturity is consistent with that of other Pristipomoides species inhabiting similar depths, emphasizing a conserved pattern of delayed maturation in these long-lived slope-dwelling snappers.

The Ornate jobfish exhibits a reproductive strategy characterized by batch spawning over an extended breeding season. At a water temperature of 20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C], field observations of gravid females and histological analysis of ovarian tissue indicate that an individual female achieves a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 2,329 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,329 eggs per day], a figure derived from annualized estimates of reproductive output. This daily fecundity reflects the species' capacity for high iteroparous investment, with spawning events occurring repeatedly throughout the warmer months. The rate of egg production is consistent with values reported for the congener Lutjanus carponotatus after correcting for differences in body mass, suggesting a conserved relationship between maternal size and reproductive allocation within the Lutjanidae. This high reproductive output helps offset the high mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval stages, a common life-history trade-off among deep-reef fishes.

The pelagic larval phase of Pristipomoides argyrogrammicus begins with the release of minute, transparent eggs into the water column. At 20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C], newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge following an incubation period of 5 days [ab = 5 days], a brief duration that reflects the elevated metabolic rates characteristic of warm-water teleost embryos. The wet weight at birth, calculated from the volume of an egg with a diameter of 0.82 millimeters, is exceptionally low at 0.00029 grams [Wwb = 0.00029 grams], a value typical of pelagic-spawning marine fishes that produce large numbers of small offspring. These lecithotrophic larvae initially rely entirely on their endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton. The rapid hatching time and minuscule neonatal mass together represent a classic r-selected reproductive strategy within the early life stages, contrasting with the extreme longevity and delayed maturation characteristic of the adult phase. This combination of high fecundity, small egg size, and brief embryonic development is a common pattern among slope-dwelling lutjanids.

The maximum wet weight attained by female Ornate jobfish during their lifetime reaches 969 grams [Wwi = 969 grams], a value observed in the largest specimens captured during deep-water fisheries surveys. This ultimate body mass is closely correlated with the asymptotic length of 40 centimeters [Li = 40 centimeters] through a length-weight relationship that has been validated across multiple geographic regions. Individuals that reach this mass are typically in the later decades of their 14,600-day lifespan (14,600 days) [am = 14,600 days], having invested the majority of their available energy into somatic growth before reproductive senescence begins to limit fecundity at a temperature of 20.4 °C [T = 20.4 °C]. In comparison to the juvenile mass at birth, the growth trajectory from 0.00029 grams [Wwb = 0.00029 grams] to nearly one kilogram represents an increase of more than three million-fold, a remarkable transformation that underscores the productivity of mesophotic reef ecosystems. The adult body size of this species makes it a valuable target for artisanal and commercial fisheries throughout its range, with the largest individuals commanding the highest market prices due to their excellent flesh quality.
